headline: Kyoto plans higher bus fares for visitors

sources.title: Kyoto unveils dual pricing for city buses and Nijo Castle (The Straits Times, from Kyodo News)
Kyoto Plans Two-Tier Prices for City Buses and Nijo Castle (Japan Cheapo)
Japanese city considers dual pricing on public transport to tackle overtourism (The Telegraph, via Yahoo News)
Kyoto plans different castle fees and bus fares for locals and visitors (The Nation Thailand)
Kyoto city bus dual pricing draft ordinance, in Japanese (Saga Shimbun, from Kyodo News)

chunks.text: A bus ride in Japan's old capital city could cost visitors almost twice what locals pay. On November 17, 2026, the city government {{put forward}} a [[draft law]] with two bus prices. The adult [[fare]], the price of one ride, is 230 yen. It would {{come down}} to 200 yen for [[residents]]. It would {{go up}} to 360 yen for [[non-residents]], people who live outside the city.

verbs.wrong: To sell a plan to a company

verbs.why: Gas prices come down when fewer people drive. Hotel rates come down after the busy season. For residents, the bus fare would come down to 200 yen.

verbs.wrong: To be printed on a ticket
verbs.why: Rents go up in many cities every year. Plane tickets go up in the summer. For non-residents, the bus fare would go up to 360 yen.

chunks.text: That group includes people from other parts of Japan, not only foreign tourists. The city calls this Japan's first such plan for public transportation. The target is [[overtourism]], when too many visitors make [[daily life]] harder for locals. In February 2025, the mayor said the city gets about 50 million [[tourist visits]] a year but has 1.5 million residents. Tourists {{pour in}}. The mayor said some residents could not {{get on}} [[packed]] buses.

verbs.correct: To arrive as a very large crowd
verbs.wrong: To vote on a new city law
verbs.why: Fans pour in when the stadium gates open. Shoppers pour in on the first day of a big sale. Tourists pour in, and the mayor said Kyoto gets about 50 million tourist visits a year.

verbs.correct: To enter a bus or train
verbs.wrong: To paint a bus or train
verbs.why: I get on the bus at the corner every morning. Passengers get on the train through the middle doors. In February 2025, the mayor said some residents could not get on packed buses.

chunks.text: The higher visitor fare would {{make up for}} the money lost on the cheaper resident fare. To get that fare, residents would have to {{sign up}} [[in advance]] and link a [[national identity card]] to a [[transit card]]. Residents paying [[in cash]] would {{miss out on}} it. For non-residents who ride often, such as [[commuters]], the city would {{give part of the difference back}} as transit points.

verbs.why: Strong December sales make up for a slow summer. A second job makes up for her lost income. The higher visitor fare would make up for the money lost on the cheaper resident fare.

verbs.wrong: To count the riders on a bus
verbs.why: Students sign up online to use the school gym. Many customers sign up to get the store's weekly deals. Residents would have to sign up in advance to get the lower bus fare.

verbs.wrong: To carry something in a bag
verbs.why: People who arrive late miss out on the free lunch. Workers who skip the meeting miss out on useful news. Residents who pay in cash would miss out on the lower fare.

verbs.display: give part of the difference back
verbs.wrong: To write something on a bus seat
verbs.why: My neighbor always gives my tools back the next day. The store gives your money back if the shoes do not fit. For non-residents who ride often, the city would give part of the difference back as transit points.

chunks.text: The city also wants two prices at a famous old castle from June 2027. A full ticket costs 1,300 yen. Non-residents would pay 2,000 yen and residents 1,000 yen. The city says the extra money would help {{fix up}} the site. Neither plan was final in November 2026. The [[city assembly]], the elected group that makes local laws, was due to {{take up}} the bus plan in a [[session]] opening on November 24. The fares would also need national government [[approval]]. The city hopes to start them in the [[budget year]] beginning April 2027.

mainIdea.s: Kyoto wants people from outside the city to pay more for its buses while residents pay less. Officials see this as a response to overtourism, and local lawmakers were due to debate it.
mainIdea.why: The city put forward a draft law with a higher fare for non-residents and a lower one for residents. The city assembly was due to take up the plan.

mainIdea.s: Japan's government has ordered foreign tourists to pay extra on buses across the country. Every Japanese rider will get a cheaper ticket, and the new prices began on November 17.
mainIdea.why: Close, but this is one city's plan, and it is not final. Anyone who lives outside Kyoto would see the fare go up, including people from other parts of Japan.

mainIdea.s: A new high-speed train will carry visitors from the airport straight to Kyoto's temples. Railway officials expect the line to cut travel times in half by the end of the decade.
mainIdea.why: There is no new train line here. Kyoto put forward a plan for two bus fares, one for residents and one for non-residents.

tf.s: Kyoto's plan would make the bus fare go up for people from outside the city.
tf.why: The fare would go up to 360 yen for non-residents, and it would be cheaper for residents.

tf.s: Only foreign tourists would pay the higher bus fare in Kyoto.
tf.why: The fare would go up for anyone who lives outside the city, including people from other parts of Japan.

tf.s: The new fares would start as soon as the city put forward the plan.
tf.why: The city hopes to start the new fares in the budget year that begins in April 2027.

tf.s: Residents would have to sign up in advance to get the lower fare.
tf.why: They would sign up and link a national identity card to a transit card.

tf.s: The higher visitor fare would make up for money lost on the resident fare.
tf.why: The higher visitor fare would make up for the money lost by cutting the resident fare.

tf.s: Residents who pay in cash would still get the lower fare.
tf.why: Residents who pay in cash would miss out on the lower fare.

lines.text: Did you see that Kyoto {{put forward}} a plan for two different bus fares?
Two fares? How would that work?
The fare would {{come down}} for people who live in the city. For everyone else, it would {{go up}} to 360 yen.
Maybe, but tourists {{pour in}} all year, and some residents can't even {{get on}} the bus.
So only foreign tourists would pay more?
No, anyone from outside the city. A visitor from another part of Japan would pay it too.
What about people who travel there for work every day?
They'd pay the higher fare, but the city would {{give part of the difference back}} as transit points.
[[It could be worse]], I guess. Do residents just show an ID?
No, they have to {{sign up}} first and link a national ID card to a transit card.
[[What a hassle]]. And if they pay cash?
Then they {{miss out on}} the lower fare.
Some people won't be happy about that.
[[You can't please everyone]]. Besides, the extra money would {{make up for}} the cheaper resident fare.
Then charging visitors more is [[not a bad idea]]. When does it start?
The city hopes to start the new fares in the budget year that begins in April 2027.
And the city assembly was due to {{take up}} the plan on November 24.
